title: Remotes: Clone, Fetch, Pull, Push —

Git 2.50.1: every command was run in the lab

toc.title: A rejected push, and the fix
Force pushes, new branches and clean-up

html:
1A remote is another repository

A remote is another Git repository that yours can send commits to and receive commits from. On GitHub it is a repository on a server. In the lab it is a bare repository, made with git init --bare: it holds the history and no working files, which is what a shared repository needs. By convention the main remote is called origin.

Command What it does
git remote add <name> <url> Connects your repository to a remote under a name
git remote -v Lists remotes with their fetch and push URLs
git clone <url> [folder] Copies a remote: history, a remote named origin, a checkout of the default branch
git push -u origin main Sends main and sets its upstream
git ls-remote origin Lists the branches and HEAD on the remote without fetching

The upstream of a branch is the remote branch it follows. It is stored as branch.main.remote and branch.main.merge, and it lets a plain git push and git pull work without arguments. A clone sets it for you.

Try it. Connect Ada's repository to the shared remote. Your hashes will differ.

git remote add origin ../shopfront.git
git remote -v
git push -u origin main
git branch -vv

origin	../shopfront.git (fetch)
origin	../shopfront.git (push)
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
* main 656c837 [origin/main] Add README
Tip

. Run git branch -vv to see which remote branch each local branch follows. The name in square brackets is the upstream.

2Fetch, pull and remote-tracking branches

origin/main is a remote-tracking branch: your own record of where main was on origin the last time you talked to it. You cannot commit on it. Only fetch, pull and push move it.

Command What it does
git fetch Downloads new commits and moves origin/*; changes no branch and no file of yours
git pull git fetch plus a merge (or a rebase) into your current branch
git pull --ff-only Pulls only if a fast-forward is possible; otherwise it stops

Ahead and behind are easy to read. git branch -vv shows [origin/main: behind 1] or [ahead 1], and git status -sb shows the same on its first line. Two ranges give the commits:

  • git log main..origin/main lists what you would get.
  • git log origin/main..main lists what you would send.

Try it. Bob looks before he changes anything.

git fetch
git branch -vv
git log --oneline main..origin/main
git pull --ff-only

   656c837..e66f90c  main       -> origin/main
* main 656c837 [origin/main: behind 1] Add README
e66f90c Add cart
Fast-forward
Tip

. Fetch whenever you like: it never changes your work. Fetch first, read the log, then decide how to integrate.

3A rejected push, and the fix

A push is accepted only if it fast-forwards the remote branch. If a teammate pushed first, the remote holds commits you lack, and Git rejects your push. The message ends with (fetch first) when you have not fetched yet, and with (non-fast-forward) after a fetch.

Try it. Reproduce it with Ada and Bob. Ada's push fails, and she fixes it.

git push
git fetch
git status -sb
git pull --rebase

 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
## main...origin/main [ahead 1, behind 1]
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main.

After that, a plain git push works. There are two honest fixes, and force is not one of them.

Fix What it does History
git pull --rebase Replays your commits on top of the fetched ones Linear
git fetch, then git merge origin/main Joins the two lines with a merge commit Keeps both lines

Plain git pull on diverged branches makes this Git stop with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches", and git pull --ff-only stops with "Not possible to fast-forward". Choose once with git config pull.rebase true to rebase on every pull, or git config pull.ff only to refuse anything but a fast-forward. Add --global to set a choice for every repository.

Tip

. A rejected push means someone pushed first: fetch and integrate, never force. Forcing throws their commits away.

4Force pushes, new branches and clean-up

A force push moves the remote branch to your version even when that discards commits.

Option Behavior
git push --force Overwrites the remote branch no matter what
git push --force-with-lease Refuses when the remote branch moved since your last fetch

In the lab Bob pushed, and Ada, who had not fetched, amended her commit. --force-with-lease refused with (stale info), but plain --force went through and Bob's commit vanished from the remote. It stayed in Bob's clone. The lease only guards what you have not fetched: after a fetch the same push passes, so look at what you are about to overwrite.

New branches. A new branch has no upstream, so git push fails with "has no upstream branch". Use git push -u origin <branch> once, or git config push.autoSetupRemote true. In the other direction, git switch <name> creates a local branch that tracks origin/<name> when only the remote one exists.

Deleting. git push origin --delete <branch> removes the branch on the remote, and your local branch stays. Teammates keep a stale origin/<branch> until they run git fetch --prune. The setting fetch.prune true does that on every fetch.

Try it. Refuse a stale force, delete a remote branch, then prune.

git push --force-with-lease
git push origin --delete feature/wishlist
git fetch --prune

 ! [rejected]        main -> main (stale info)
 - [deleted]         feature/wishlist
 - [deleted]         (none)     -> origin/feature/wishlist
Tip

. Use git push --force-with-lease, never plain --force. It refuses when someone else pushed first.

5More than one remote

A repository can have several remotes. The common second name is upstream: the original repository when you work from your own copy (module 8). Each remote has its own remote-tracking branches, such as upstream/main.

Command What it does
git remote add upstream <url> Adds a second remote
git fetch upstream Fetches from that remote only
git push upstream main Pushes to that remote by name
git remote set-url origin <url> Changes where a remote points, for example after a move
git remote get-url origin Prints the URL a remote uses

Try it. Add a second remote and look at the refs on it.

git remote add upstream ../upstream_shop.git
git remote -v
git push upstream main
git ls-remote --heads upstream

origin	../shopfront.git (fetch)
origin	../shopfront.git (push)
upstream	../upstream_shop.git (fetch)
upstream	../upstream_shop.git (push)
2db54f0d6c1ed783cb292bea9cad5545dfaede87	refs/heads/main
Tip

. Name the remote in every command when you have two. git push upstream main and git push origin main do different things.

6Practice Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1After git fetch, git branch -vv shows * main 656c837 [origin/main: behind 1] Add README. What is true now?

  • AYour working files already contain the new commit
  • BYour main branch still points at the old commit
  • CThe remote deleted its own copy of the branch
  • DA merge commit was created on your main branch
Show the answer

Answer: B. Fetch only moves origin/main, so you are one commit behind until you merge or pull.

S2Bob's git push is rejected, and the message ends with (fetch first). What should he do?

  • ARun git push --force to replace the remote branch
  • BRun git push -u origin main to set the upstream
  • CRun git remote set-url origin with a new address
  • DRun git fetch, merge or rebase, then push again
Show the answer

Answer: D. The remote has commits he lacks, so he fetches, rebases or merges them in, and pushes again.

S3Ada runs git push --force-with-lease and Git prints (stale info). What does that mean?

  • AThe remote branch moved since her last fetch
  • BHer branch does not have an upstream set yet
  • CHer local branch has no new commits to send
  • DThe remote refuses every force push by policy
Show the answer

Answer: A. The lease compares the remote with her last fetch, and a teammate's push made them differ.

S4git log origin/main..main prints two commits. What does that tell you?

  • ATwo commits on origin are missing from your branch
  • BYour branch and origin have two merge conflicts
  • CTwo commits exist on your branch that origin lacks
  • DTwo commits were removed from origin by a prune
Show the answer

Answer: C. The range lists commits reachable from main but not from origin/main, which are the ones a push would send.

S5The team wants a plain git pull to replay local commits on top of fetched ones and keep history linear. Which setting does that?

  • Agit config pull.ff only, which refuses all but fast-forwards
  • Bgit config pull.rebase true, which rebases on every pull
  • Cgit config fetch.prune true, which prunes on every fetch
  • Dgit config push.autoSetupRemote true, which sets upstreams
Show the answer

Answer: B. With pull.rebase true, a pull fetches and then rebases the local commits instead of merging.

S6Ada deleted feature/wishlist with git push origin --delete feature/wishlist. Bob's git branch -r still lists origin/feature/wishlist. How does he remove it?

  • Agit fetch --prune, which drops stale tracking branches
  • Bgit pull --ff-only, which updates his current branch only
  • Cgit branch -d feature/wishlist, which deletes a local branch
  • Dgit restore origin/feature/wishlist, which restores a file
Show the answer

Answer: A. A plain fetch keeps stale remote-tracking branches, and --prune removes the ones whose remote branch is gone.

6.2 Recall questions

R1Which command connects an existing repository to a remote named origin?

Show the answer

git remote add origin <url>.

R2What does the -u in git push -u origin main set up?

Show the answer

The upstream, so a plain git push and git pull work later.

R3What does git pull do?

Show the answer

It runs git fetch and then merges, or rebases, into the current branch.

R4What does origin/main record?

Show the answer

Where main was on origin at your last fetch, push or pull.

R5Which push option is safer than --force?

Show the answer

--force-with-lease.

R6Which command changes the URL a remote points to?

Show the answer

git remote set-url <name> <url>.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Remote another repository; the lab uses a bare one; origin is the usual name
Setup git remote add, git remote -v, git clone, git push -u origin main
Tracking the upstream is set by a clone or push -u; git branch -vv shows it
Fetch and pull fetch only moves origin/*; pull is fetch plus merge or rebase; --ff-only refuses anything else
Ahead and behind git status -sb, git branch -vv; main..origin/main to get, origin/main..main to send
Rejected push someone pushed first: fetch, then pull --rebase or merge, then push
Force --force-with-lease refuses after others pushed; plain --force overwrites
Clean-up git push origin --delete <branch>; git fetch --prune; fetch.prune true
Several remotes git remote add upstream, git fetch upstream, set-url, ls-remote
